input: The condition that governs phase equilibrium can be stated quite simply, although its consequences are far-reaching. For a binary mixture held at fixed pressure, equilibrium between the phases requires that the chemical potential of each component be identical in every phase in which the component is present. The chemical potential may be thought of as a measure of the escaping tendency of a component from a phase: if the value in one phase exceeds the value in the other, there is a net driving force for the component to migrate across the boundary, and migration continues, with the compositions of both phases adjusting as it proceeds, until the two values come into balance. Because the pressure is held constant throughout, the system accommodates itself by way of temperature and composition rather than by way of pressure, and at any given temperature the compositions that the liquid and the vapour adopt at equilibrium are determined by the condition itself. It follows that equilibrium is a simultaneous requirement, applying to all components at once, and that a departure from equality for any one component is sufficient to set the system in motion again. The statement is general: it does not depend on the identity of the components involved.
target: Phase equilibrium for a binary mixture at fixed pressure rests on a single condition, stated in words before any equation is named: at equilibrium, the chemical potential of each component is the same in every phase in which that component appears. Chemical potential measures the tendency of a component to leave a phase. Where its value in one phase stands above its value in another, the component passes from the phase with the higher value to the phase with the lower, and the composition of both phases changes as it moves. The transfer stops when the values meet, and it stops for every component at the same state, since the phases share one temperature and one pressure throughout. Pressure is held fixed, so the adjustment falls on temperature and on the compositions: at a chosen temperature, the equilibrium compositions of the liquid and the vapour are fixed by the condition, and neither phase can hold an arbitrary composition while the other keeps its own. Away from equilibrium, the condition gives the direction of change as well as the end state, because the sign of the difference in chemical potential between the phases sets the direction in which each component moves. A mixture is at equilibrium only when the condition holds for every component at once; equality for one component alongside inequality for the other is a state still in motion.
